paragraphs: Text-image models can classify images using descriptions of candidate categories, but the wording of those descriptions affects accuracy. Combining several prompts can help, yet choosing them often requires manual work. This paper asks whether a model can automatically select and weight useful prompts from a large pool without labeled validation examples.

The authors identify problems with a naive scoring approach: biases in pretraining and test data can make a prompt appear more reliable than it actually is. They introduce a scoring method that corrects for these biases, then use the scores to form a weighted prompt ensemble. The key idea is to distinguish apparent confidence from evidence that a prompt suits the downstream dataset.

The resulting method performs better overall than equal-weight prompt averaging and hand-crafted prompts across ImageNet, four variants, and eleven fine-grained classification benchmarks. The procedure is automatic and requires neither optimization nor labeled validation data. These findings support prompt weighting as a practical way to improve zero-shot classification, while the reported overall advantage does not imply that every individual dataset improves.
icml-2023-a-simple-zero-shot-prompt-weig.tldr: Automatically correcting biased prompt scores improves weighted prompt ensembles without optimization or labeled validation data.

paragraphs: Generating images from very few training examples makes coverage especially important: ignoring even part of a small dataset discards substantial information. GANs can suffer from mode collapse, concentrating on a subset of examples. Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation, or IMLE, uses the same kind of generator with a different training objective intended to encourage broader coverage.

The paper addresses a restriction in IMLE's theoretical foundation. Its existing guarantees require the optimal likelihood to be identical at every data point. The authors develop a more general formulation that contains the original method as a special case and prove guarantees under weaker conditions. This broadens the circumstances covered by the theory without claiming that guarantees hold without conditions.

From that formulation, they derive Adaptive IMLE, an algorithm that responds to differences in how difficult individual examples are to learn. On multiple few-shot image synthesis datasets, it significantly outperforms existing methods. The contribution therefore connects a less restrictive mathematical justification with an adaptive training procedure, addressing the problem of learning from scarce examples without treating all examples as equally difficult.
icml-2023-adaptive-imle-for-few-shot-pre.tldr: Adaptive IMLE weakens earlier theoretical restrictions and adapts to example difficulty to improve few-shot image generation.

paragraphs: The Arcade Learning Environment evaluates reinforcement learning algorithms across 57 games, but running the full suite is computationally expensive. That cost limits how often researchers can use the benchmark and reproduce results. This paper develops a principled way to select a much smaller collection of environments that still represents performance across the larger suite.

Applying the method produces Atari-5, a subset of five games. The authors report that this subset estimates the full suite's median score within 10% of its actual value. A larger subset of ten games recovers 80% of the variance in log-scores across all 57 games. These are two distinct measures of how much information a reduced benchmark preserves.

The explanation is that performance on many ALE games is highly correlated, so the full suite contains substantial overlapping information. Carefully chosen games can therefore stand in for part of that repeated evidence. The findings support cheaper estimates of broad benchmark performance; the stated results concern median scores and log-score variance, rather than exact reconstruction of every game's result.
icml-2023-atari-5-distilling-the-arcade-.tldr: A carefully selected five-game Atari subset estimates the full 57-game median score within 10%.

paragraphs: Assessing adversarial robustness requires understanding predictions throughout a set of possible inputs. BNN-DP tackles this problem for Bayesian neural networks by computing lower and upper prediction bounds that hold for every point in a specified compact input set. This makes the prediction range, rather than a few sampled outputs, the central object of analysis.

The framework treats a Bayesian neural network as a stochastic dynamical system evolving across layers. That interpretation allows dynamic programming to organize the bounding calculation. Bound propagation and convex relaxations produce a backward recursion, using piecewise affine functions to enclose the possible prediction range. The enclosure is an over-approximation, so it is designed to contain the range rather than reproduce it exactly.

BNN-DP supports both regression and classification. Across the tested tasks and network architectures, the authors report improvements of up to four orders of magnitude over state-of-the-art methods in bound tightness and computational efficiency. Tighter bounds provide a more informative robustness assessment, while faster computation makes that assessment more practical. The reported maximum improvements describe the experiments, not a uniform gain for every network.
icml-2023-bnn-dp-robustness-certificatio.tldr: BNN-DP uses dynamic programming to efficiently bound Bayesian neural network predictions over entire input sets.

paragraphs: A treatment can affect different people differently, so causal analysis often aims to estimate average effects conditional on observed characteristics. Meta-learners organize this estimation around supervised learning methods without committing to a particular predictive model. The paper examines what happens when treatments have several possible levels rather than just two.

Moving beyond binary treatment introduces difficulties that straightforward extensions of existing meta-learners do not always handle well. The authors analyze upper bounds on estimation error, explicitly examining how those bounds depend on quantities such as the number of treatment levels. This provides a way to study how an estimator's theoretical behavior changes as the treatment choices become more numerous.

The paper also introduces and discusses meta-learners that perform well as the number of treatments grows. Experiments using synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets confirm strengths and weaknesses among the methods. The combined theoretical and empirical analysis matters because flexibility in choosing a supervised learner does not by itself ensure a good extension to multiple treatments. The results help distinguish approaches whose handling of treatment levels remains effective from naive extensions that can become unsatisfactory.
icml-2023-comparison-of-meta-learners-fo.tldr: The paper analyzes and compares meta-learners for multiple treatment levels, showing why naive binary-treatment extensions can be inadequate.

paragraphs: Choosing an intervention involves more than predicting what will happen: the intervention should improve a target while satisfying constraints. This paper introduces constrained causal Bayesian optimization, or cCBO, for that task when the causal graph is known. The graph provides information about how changing one variable can affect other quantities of interest.

The method first uses graph structure, together with observational data when available, to reduce the intervention search space. It then models target and constraint quantities with Gaussian processes. A constrained expected improvement rule selects interventions sequentially, combining the search for better outcomes with consideration of feasibility. This organizes the optimization around both causal structure and the constraints on acceptable interventions.

The authors propose several surrogate models that combine observational and interventional data and capture correlations between effects at different levels of sophistication. Evaluations on artificial and real-world causal graphs show a successful trade-off between convergence speed and the proportion of feasible interventions. The findings support using causal information to guide constrained experimentation, with the known causal graph serving as an explicit prerequisite of the proposed approach.
icml-2023-constrained-causal-bayesian-op.tldr: cCBO uses a known causal graph and probabilistic models to search efficiently for interventions that improve a target while respecting constraints.

paragraphs: Many convergence analyses assume that each training sample is drawn independently from the target distribution. This paper studies constrained, smooth, nonconvex optimization when successive samples can depend on one another. Its main focus is stochastic projected gradient methods, with a mild mixing condition replacing independent sampling. That condition holds for a broad class of Markov chain sampling algorithms.

The authors establish a worst-case convergence rate of approximately t to the power of minus one quarter, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Reaching an epsilon-near stationary point requires approximately epsilon to the power of minus four steps, improving the previous dependence of minus eight. Stationarity is measured through the Moreau-envelope gradient and gradient mapping; the guarantee concerns approaching stationarity rather than finding a global optimum.

The analysis also yields dependent-data convergence results for stochastic proximal gradient methods, AdaGrad, and heavy-ball momentum. As an application, the authors develop online nonnegative matrix factorization algorithms using adaptive step sizes and report an optimal convergence rate. The broader contribution is a simpler analysis that accommodates dependence while substantially strengthening the stated complexity guarantee.
icml-2023-convergence-of-first-order-met.tldr: Under a mild mixing condition, the paper strengthens convergence guarantees for constrained nonconvex optimization with dependent samples.

paragraphs: In distributed linear regression, different parties hold different portions of the data. This paper considers a privacy-preserving arrangement in which those parties share selected summary statistics after adding noise. The inference problem is therefore to estimate regression coefficients from privately released summaries, accounting for the statistical structure of what has been shared.

The authors build a generative statistical model for these noisy statistics. It uses a distributional relationship between the summary quantities involved in linear regression, allowing the estimation procedure to exploit their connections. They then develop Bayesian inference for the regression coefficients, primarily through Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms. This makes the model for the shared statistics an explicit part of the inference framework.

The paper also offers a faster alternative that produces an approximate Bayesian estimate in one iteration. The proposed methods have computational advantages over competing approaches, and numerical evaluations on real and simulated data show well-rounded estimation and prediction. The contribution combines a model of privacy-preserving summaries with both sampling-based and fast approximate inference, addressing computation alongside the quality of regression results.
icml-2023-differentially-private-distrib.tldr: A statistical model of privately shared summaries enables distributed Bayesian linear regression with MCMC and a fast approximate alternative.

paragraphs: An expert may be reliable on one kind of problem and much less knowledgeable on another. Combining advice without accounting for that variation can produce poor decisions and may disadvantage minority cases. This paper models expertise as varying across regions of the problem space, so the relevant question is which expert fits the particular case.

The authors first consider a simple approach based on nearest-neighbor queries and identify its drawbacks. They then introduce expertise trees, which use decision trees to enable a learner to select appropriate models. The approach explicitly adapts to the relationship between the problem instance and the experts' knowledge, rather than treating expertise as a single fixed property.

The paper provides theoretical insights and empirical evaluations across problems where existing methods were inadequate. Those evaluations show improved performance for the proposed approach. The significance is that collective decision-making can benefit from organizing knowledge by where it applies. Although discriminatory decisions motivate the work, the stated findings establish improved performance on the evaluated problems rather than a universal guarantee of fair decisions.
icml-2023-expertise-trees-resolve-knowle.tldr: Expertise trees improve collective decisions by selecting models according to how their expertise fits each problem instance.

paragraphs: Energy-based models are often trained using samples from Markov chains, but practical training may use chains that stop before reaching equilibrium. This paper analyzes what such incomplete sampling does to learning. It focuses on short, non-persistent runs used to estimate training gradients, including the strategy of restarting from random initial conditions.

The central analytical finding is that a trained model can perfectly reproduce a set of empirical data statistics through a particular dynamical process, even when its equilibrium distribution does not reproduce them. This separates two notions of success: what a short sampling procedure generates and what the model would generate at equilibrium. The distinction explains how short-run sampling can work well despite not converging.

After presenting the argument for generic energy-based models, the authors examine two solvable models to describe how non-convergent sampling affects learned parameters. They test their predictions numerically on a convolutional-network energy model and a Boltzmann machine. The results offer a first-principles explanation for previously observed high-quality short-run samples and provide groundwork for treating energy-based models as diffusion models.
icml-2023-explaining-the-effects-of-non-.tldr: Short-run training can make energy-based models reproduce data statistics through sampling dynamics rather than their equilibrium distribution.

paragraphs: Hypothesis transfer learning reuses a model learned on a source task when learning a target task, without needing the original source data. This is useful when retaining or accessing large datasets is burdensome. The paper studies the theoretical behavior of this transfer approach for binary classification, where establishing learning guarantees poses particular challenges.

The authors focus on regularized empirical risk minimizers and analyze them through algorithmic stability. This framework examines how sensitive a learning procedure is to changes in its training data. Under mild assumptions, the analysis supplies learning guarantees for the transfer setting, connecting the behavior of the training algorithm to its statistical performance.

The resulting generalization bounds are complexity-free and address training error, excess risk, and cross-validation estimates. They also allow the behavior of standard surrogate classification losses to be compared across different scenarios. The contribution is a theoretical basis for understanding the benefits of transferring a learned hypothesis and the consequences of loss-function choice. Those guarantees remain conditional on the analysis's assumptions rather than establishing that transfer always improves a target task.
icml-2023-hypothesis-transfer-learning-w.tldr: Algorithmic stability yields generalization guarantees for binary classification that transfers a source model without accessing its training data.

paragraphs: Causal representation learning aims to recover meaningful hidden factors from low-level observations. Many approaches rely on observational data together with assumptions about how the factors are related. This paper investigates a different source of information: interventions can change the geometry of the values that hidden factors are able to take.

The key observation concerns support, meaning the set of possible values of a factor. When factors are causally connected, an intervention can break the dependence of an intervened factor's support on its ancestors. The authors use these geometric signatures to prove identification results. With data from perfect do interventions, latent causal factors can be recovered up to permutation and scaling, leaving their ordering and scale undetermined.

For imperfect interventions, the paper establishes block affine identification: recovered factors may remain mixed with a limited group of other factors. These results show how intervention data can support provable recovery without assumptions about the factors' distributions or dependency structure. The distinction between perfect and imperfect interventions matters because it determines the strength of identification claimed by the analysis.
icml-2023-interventional-causal-represen.tldr: Geometric information from interventions enables provable recovery of latent causal factors, with stronger identification for perfect interventions.

paragraphs: Deep networks contain many nonlinear units, but their usefulness may change over training. This paper empirically investigates how far a network can be simplified toward a linear function before performance collapses. The authors apply a sparsity preference to the number of nonlinear units, fully linearizing selected feature channels in image classification and machine translation models.

The timing of simplification makes a substantial difference. Removing nonlinearity early produces a significant performance gap compared with doing so late in training. After training, many nonlinear units can be linearized while high performance remains. This suggests that some expressive capacity helps gradient descent during early learning even when the final learned function does not need all of that capacity.

To describe the simplified networks, the authors introduce average path length: the average number of active nonlinearities encountered along a path through the network. Under sparsity pressure, the remaining nonlinear units form structured core networks with nearly constant effective depth and width that depend on task difficulty. These empirical findings distinguish the nonlinearity useful for learning from the nonlinearity retained in an effective trained solution.
icml-2023-nonlinear-advantage-trained-ne.tldr: Experiments show that many nonlinear units can be removed after training while preserving high performance, although early removal is more damaging.

paragraphs: Distributed learning may need to protect honest participants' data while tolerating machines that behave adversarially. These goals have often been studied separately. This paper analyzes their combined effect on utility, expressed through the error incurred by algorithms that provide both differential privacy and robustness against a fraction of adversarial machines.

The authors establish a tight trade-off by proving both a lower bound and a matching upper bound. The lower-bound argument studies mean estimation under distributed privacy and robustness requirements, reducing it to centralized estimation of one-way marginals. It identifies an error cost that any algorithm meeting the stated requirements must incur, rather than a weakness of one particular implementation.

To match that lower bound, the paper introduces a distributed learning algorithm with a high-dimensional robust aggregation rule. The rule amortizes the dimension dependence in the error caused jointly by adversarial workers and privacy, without relying on the data's statistical properties. Together, the bounds characterize both an unavoidable cost and an attainable performance level, clarifying why privacy, robustness, and utility cannot be optimized independently in this setting.
icml-2023-on-the-privacy-robustness-util.tldr: Matching error bounds characterize a fundamental trade-off between privacy, adversarial robustness, and utility in distributed learning.

paragraphs: Standard self-attention becomes costly on long sequences because its memory and computation grow quadratically with sequence length. Malware classification motivates this paper, with sequences of at least 100,000 elements creating a major obstacle. The authors reformulate attention using Holographic Reduced Representations, a neuro-symbolic approach, and implement the result as Hrrformer.

The reformulation preserves attention's high-level operation: queries match against keys and retrieve weighted information from values. Its time complexity is O(T H log H), and its space complexity is O(T H), where T denotes sequence length and H the representation dimension. For fixed H, both scale linearly with sequence length, addressing the quadratic growth that makes ordinary attention difficult to apply.

The authors report convergence in ten times fewer epochs, near state-of-the-art accuracy on Long Range Arena, and successful learning with a single layer. Training is up to 280 times faster on that benchmark. They also report viability for the very long malware sequences motivating the work. These results combine favorable computational scaling with empirical accuracy, rather than claiming identical behavior to standard attention.
icml-2023-recasting-self-attention-with-.tldr: Hrrformer reformulates attention to scale linearly with sequence length while retaining strong long-sequence benchmark accuracy.

paragraphs: Online changepoint detection looks for changes as observations arrive, making the cost of repeated updates central to its usefulness. This paper proposes a Bayesian approach that combines provable robustness with scalability. It addresses the difficulty of obtaining both properties in one procedure, rather than treating robustness and efficient updating as separate objectives.

The method uses a generalized Bayesian formulation together with diffusion score matching. This combination produces conjugate posteriors whose parameters have closed-form expressions. In practical terms, the posterior update can be carried out through simple algebra. The mathematical construction therefore supplies both the robustness guarantee and a tractable form for the ongoing inference calculations.

The resulting algorithm is exact within the proposed formulation, and the authors report that it runs more than ten times faster than its closest competitor. Exactness here describes computation under that formulation, while robustness is a separately established property. The contribution is a route to robust Bayesian changepoint analysis whose updates remain computationally simple, directly addressing the scalability problems associated with earlier attempts.
icml-2023-robust-and-scalable-bayesian-o.tldr: A generalized Bayesian changepoint detector combines provable robustness, exact algebraic updates, and a reported speedup exceeding tenfold.

paragraphs: Sharpness Aware Minimization, or SAM, was motivated by penalizing sharp minima, and much of its analysis has focused on behavior near those minima. This paper argues that an important part of SAM's operation occurs throughout training. It finds strong regulation of Hessian eigenvalues, quantities that describe curvature of the loss, along the learning trajectory.

In a simplified setting, the authors show that SAM dynamically induces a stabilization related to the edge-of-stability phenomenon seen in gradient descent with large learning rates. Their theory predicts the largest eigenvalue as a function of the learning rate and SAM radius. This connects curvature control to the optimizer's evolving dynamics and its parameters.

The authors also show that practical models can exhibit this stabilization. The result changes how SAM's behavior should be interpreted: analyzing only the geometry of a final minimum misses effects that occur far from any minimum. The simplified theory and practical observations support a dynamical account of eigenvalue regularization, while the practical finding is that this behavior can occur, rather than that every model must display it.
icml-2023-sam-operates-far-from-home-eig.tldr: SAM controls loss curvature throughout training through dynamics linked to edge-of-stability behavior, not just through behavior near minima.

paragraphs: Generative sequence models can process tokens representing text, speech, images, and other data types. This paper studies how such mixed-modal models scale when modalities are trained together. The authors conduct more than 250 experiments across seven modalities, using models from 8 million to 30 billion parameters and training sets of 5–100 billion tokens.

They develop scaling laws that account for both individual modalities and their interactions. An added term represents synergy and competition associated with data and model size, extending earlier single-modality laws. This matters because the behavior of a shared model depends not only on each modality's contribution, but also on how the modalities help or compete with one another.

The study reports empirical training phenomena, including naturally alternating progress across modalities, guidance for important hyperparameters, and links between competition and training stability. As a test of the scaling law, the authors train a 30-billion-parameter speech-text model that significantly outperforms the corresponding unimodal models. The findings provide empirical guidance for designing and training mixed-modal models while explicitly accounting for interactions between their data types.
icml-2023-scaling-laws-for-generative-mi.tldr: Mixed-modal scaling laws model how modalities cooperate and compete as training data and model size increase.

paragraphs: With large gradient-descent steps, training often shows increasing loss curvature followed by stabilization near the convergence boundary. These patterns are called progressive sharpening and the edge of stability. They do not occur in the constant neural tangent kernel regime, where predictions are approximately linear in the parameters. The paper therefore studies models whose predictions are quadratic in their parameters.

For quadratic objectives in two dimensions, the authors prove that these second-order regression models exhibit progressive sharpening of the neural tangent kernel eigenvalue. They explicitly calculate its limiting value, which differs slightly from the edge of stability. The result supplies a tractable nonlinear setting in which sharpening can be mathematically established.

In higher dimensions, the models generally show similar behavior even without a neural network's particular structure. This suggests that sharpening and edge-of-stability dynamics may belong to a broader class of discrete learning algorithms applied to high-dimensional nonlinear models. The paper thus separates these phenomena from neural-network-specific architecture, while presenting their broader generality as a possibility supported by the observed behavior rather than a universal theorem.
icml-2023-second-order-regression-models.tldr: Quadratic-in-parameter regression models exhibit sharpening near the stability boundary, suggesting these dynamics extend beyond neural networks.

paragraphs: Extreme classification involves choosing labels from thousands or even millions of classes. In its zero-shot form, a model must handle new classes without additional supervision. SemSup-XC addresses this by representing classes through automatically collected descriptions, giving the model information about what a class means even when labeled examples for it are unavailable.

The model uses a hybrid matching module that compares an input with class descriptions through both semantic and lexical similarity. This combines matching by meaning with matching based on wording. Contrastive learning trains the model around these relationships. The approach makes the content of a class description a central part of classification, rather than treating each class only as an identifier.

Across three datasets drawn from legal, e-commerce, and Wikipedia data, SemSup-XC achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot and few-shot performance. Reported gains reach 12 precision points in zero-shot tests and exceed 10 points in one-shot tests, with similar improvements in recall@10. Ablations highlight the contributions of the hybrid matching module and collected descriptions, supporting both components' importance in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-semsup-xc-semantic-supervision.tldr: SemSup-XC combines class descriptions with semantic and lexical matching to improve zero-shot and few-shot extreme classification.

paragraphs: Instrumental-variable methods estimate causal effects when hidden confounding is present and direct treatment experiments are unavailable. Instruments affect the outcome only through the treatment variables. Standard applications typically require at least as many instruments as treatments, which becomes restrictive when many treatment dimensions must be studied using only a few experimental instruments.

With too few instruments, a single experiment cannot identify the complete treatment effect, even in a linear setting. The paper shows that useful information can still be recovered: the projection of the effect onto the instrumented subspace. This is the component of the overall effect accessible through the available instruments, giving a precise target for partial estimation.

The authors develop techniques to combine partial estimates consistently across different instrument sets. They then use those combined estimators in a sequential algorithm that proposes informative instruments for the next experimental round. The goal is to maximize accumulated information about the full causal effect. The contribution makes incomplete experiments useful and coordinates their information, without claiming that any single underspecified experiment identifies the entire effect.
icml-2023-sequential-underspecified-inst.tldr: Partial causal effects from limited instruments can be combined across experiments to guide more informative instrument selection.

paragraphs: Repeatedly applying privacy mechanisms to sensitive data requires tracking their combined privacy guarantees. This paper studies that accounting problem when the number of compositions is large. Its goal is an accurate approximation of the privacy curve that remains computationally inexpensive, using analytical expressions rather than relying entirely on numerical computation.

The authors transform the privacy-loss random variable through exponential tilting and express the privacy curve as a contour integral. The integration path has an adjustable real-axis intercept. Choosing that intercept at a saddle point enables the method of steepest descent to produce accurate closed-form approximations. They call the resulting procedure the saddle-point accountant, or SPA.

SPA provides a constant-time approximation of the privacy curve. The theoretical results refine ideas associated with Gaussian Differential Privacy and the moments accountant in Rényi Differential Privacy. Numerical experiments show approximation precision competitive with numerical approaches such as FFT-based accountants. The contribution is therefore a mathematically explicit and efficient accounting method for large compositions, with its output described as an accurate approximation rather than an exact evaluation.
icml-2023-the-saddle-point-method-in-dif.tldr: The saddle-point accountant gives accurate, constant-time approximations of privacy guarantees when many mechanisms are composed.

paragraphs: Kernel machines can be competitive with deep neural networks on small datasets, but scaling them creates a structural difficulty. In traditional kernel methods, model size is tied to the amount of training data. This coupling makes larger datasets computationally challenging, whereas neural networks can vary model size and training-set size independently.

The paper develops general kernel models that separate those two choices. Its central algorithm, EigenPro 3.0, uses projected dual preconditioned stochastic gradient descent to train these models. The aim is to make large-data kernel learning feasible without requiring model size to track dataset size in the traditional way. Decoupling the model and data is the organizing contribution.

The authors demonstrate scaling to model and dataset sizes that existing kernel methods had not supported. They also provide a PyTorch implementation capable of using multiple GPUs. These findings concern the computational reach of kernel learning, expanding the sizes at which such models can be trained. The abstract's small-data accuracy motivation does not establish that the new large-scale models universally outperform deep neural networks.
icml-2023-toward-large-kernel-models-b09.tldr: EigenPro 3.0 scales general kernel models by decoupling model size from training-data size.

paragraphs: Path attribution methods explain model predictions by assigning importance to input features, with principles motivated by game theory. Yet satisfying formal axioms does not necessarily prevent counter-intuitive explanations. This paper investigates why such problems arise in deep visual models and why their computed attributions may depart from the game-theoretic intuitions behind the framework.

The authors identify conditions under which counter-intuitive attributions can be avoided. They also develop a mechanism for integrating attributions over paths so that the computation conforms to the original game-theoretic insights. Combining these findings yields an attribution method intended to provide intuitive and reliable explanations. The work connects the framework's conceptual justification to the details of how explanations are actually computed.

Evaluations span multiple datasets, models, and metrics, with consistent quantitative and qualitative improvements over baselines. These results support the proposed method across the tested settings. The theoretical contribution is conditional: it identifies circumstances that avoid the problematic attributions. Together, the analysis and experiments show why credible visual explanations require attention to both attribution principles and the integration procedure used to implement them.
icml-2023-towards-credible-visual-model-.tldr: The paper refines path attribution to avoid identified counter-intuitive explanations and better match its game-theoretic foundations.

paragraphs: A language model may imitate an individual convincingly while failing to reproduce behavior across a population. This paper introduces Turing Experiments to assess that broader question. Each experiment asks a model to simulate a representative sample of participants in a human-subject study, allowing researchers to check established findings and identify systematic distortions.

The authors design a simulation methodology and apply it to four classic settings: the Ultimatum Game, Garden Path Sentences, the Milgram Shock Experiment, and Wisdom of Crowds. These span economic behavior, language processing, and social psychology. Comparing language models on the same experimental tasks provides a way to evaluate which aspects of human behavior their simulations reproduce.

Recent models replicate the existing findings in the first three experiments. The Wisdom of Crowds experiment instead exposes a hyper-accuracy distortion in some models, including ChatGPT and GPT-4. This shows that successful replication in several settings can coexist with a systematic mismatch elsewhere. The authors suggest that such distortion could affect applications in education and the arts, making population-level behavioral tests useful for understanding the scope of human simulation.
icml-2023-using-large-language-models-to.tldr: Turing Experiments test simulated populations, finding both replication of human-study results and systematic hyper-accuracy in some language models.
